title: New Hampshire Civics (12th Grade)
description: New Hampshire Civics (12th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: A Concord student asks why no state law, however popular, can override the United States Constitution. The reason is that the Constitution is:
questions.correctAnswer: The supreme law of the land - the highest legal authority in the United States
distractors: A set of guidelines states may follow or ignore
Only a historical document with no legal force today
Equal in authority to any state statute
questions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws and treaties the supreme law of the land. Judges in every state are bound by it, so a state rule that conflicts with it cannot stand - the founding answer to the weak confederation that came before.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Supreme means nothing sits above it.

img.scene: A tall granite courthouse tower rising above a small New England city at dawn, flag flying from its peak. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Supreme means nothing sits above it.

questions.question: New citizens in Manchester take their oath beneath a banner showing the Constitution's famous first three words. A student asks what big idea those words declare about who ultimately holds power in America. Government power comes from:
questions.correctAnswer: The consent of the governed - the people themselves
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty is the Constitution's first idea: authority flows upward from the people, who created the government in 1788 and remain its source. Every later article only distributes power the people granted.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: We the People - power starts with us.

img.scene: A diverse crowd of citizens gathered on a green in front of a white New England meetinghouse, morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: We the People - power starts with us.
img.title: WE THE PEOPLE

questions.question: More than two centuries of change have produced a known total of constitutional amendments - the first ten arrived as one package in 1791. What is the complete count in force today?
questions.correctAnswer: 27 amendments
questions.explanation: The first ten amendments (the Bill of Rights) were added in 1791, and seventeen more followed over two centuries - the most recent, the 27th on congressional pay, was ratified in 1992 after being proposed in 1789.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten at first, twenty-seven in all.

img.scene: A long marble corridor in a grand civic building with many framed panels receding into soft light, all frames blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Ten at first, twenty-seven in all.
img.title: TWENTY-SEVEN AMENDMENTS

questions.question: A proposed amendment is approved by two-thirds of both houses of Congress. What must happen next for it to become part of the Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: Three-fourths of the states must ratify it
distractors: A national popular vote must approve it
The Supreme Court must uphold it first
questions.explanation: Article V sets two hurdles: proposal (usually by two-thirds of Congress) and ratification by three-fourths of the states - currently 38 of 50. The President plays no role in amending the Constitution at all.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths decide.

img.scene: A map-like mosaic of many small colored stone tiles forming one large shield shape on a civic plaza floor, no labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds propose, three-fourths decide.
img.title: HOW AMENDMENTS ARE RATIFIED

questions.question: A state passes a tax that Congress has expressly forbidden states to levy. A court strikes the tax down. This is the Constitution's system of:
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism - power divided between national and state governments, with federal law supreme in its sphere
questions.explanation: Federalism splits authority: the national government holds enumerated powers, the states hold reserved powers, and where valid federal law speaks, it prevails. Most day-to-day governance - schools, roads, police - still sits with the states.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two levels of government, one supreme in its lane.

img.scene: Two interlocking stone archways of different heights forming one gateway over a country road. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Two levels of government, one supreme in its lane.
img.title: FEDERALISM AT WORK

questions.question: Police powers, public schools and driver's licenses are powers the Constitution leaves mainly to the states. The amendment that reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Tenth Amendment
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment closes the Bill of Rights with the federal bargain in one sentence: powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states or to the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: What is not given is kept - the Tenth says so.

img.scene: A sturdy stone wall with a gate standing open onto green fields and a small town beyond. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: What is not given is kept - the Tenth says so.
img.title: THE TENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: Congress taxes imports, a power the Constitution grants it expressly, while a state tries to tax the same imports at its port. The state tax fails because import taxation is:
questions.correctAnswer: An exclusive federal power - the Constitution denies it to the states
distractors: A concurrent power both levels may use freely
A local power reserved to port cities
Permitted if the governor approves it
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 10 lists powers denied to the states, including taxing imports or exports without Congress's consent. Some powers are shared (concurrent), but this one is fenced off to keep a single national trade policy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Some powers are fenced - imports are one.

img.scene: A busy harbor with tall ships and cranes at golden hour, one flag flying over the customs house. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Some powers are fenced - imports are one.
img.title: POWERS DENIED TO STATES

questions.question: A governor argues that because the Constitution lists Congress's powers, Congress may do nothing beyond the literal list. The strongest reply rests on the Necessary and Proper Clause, which:
questions.correctAnswer: Lets Congress make laws needed to carry out its listed powers, as upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
distractors: Lets the President legislate in emergencies
Gives states a veto over federal laws
Was removed by the Tenth Amendment
questions.explanation: In McCulloch v. Maryland the Supreme Court read the elastic clause broadly - Congress may choose means reasonably related to its enumerated ends - and barred Maryland from taxing the national bank, because the power to tax is the power to destroy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elastic clause: ends listed, means implied.

img.scene: A wide river flowing under a stone bridge with many arches, a mill town on the far bank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Elastic clause: ends listed, means implied.
img.title: NECESSARY AND PROPER

questions.question: Two states dispute a river boundary and one sues the other directly in the Supreme Court. The Court may hear the case first - rather than on appeal - because the Constitution gives it:
questions.correctAnswer: Original jurisdiction over cases involving states
questions.explanation: Article III gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors and those in which a state is a party; everything else reaches it on appeal. State-versus-state suits are the classic original-jurisdiction cases.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: States sue states at the top court directly.

img.scene: Two riverbanks facing each other across calm water with a survey marker stone in the middle distance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: States sue states at the top court directly.
img.title: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION

questions.question: A president serves two full terms and asks whether a third election run is allowed in an emergency. The answer, since 1951, comes from the:
questions.correctAnswer: Twenty-second Amendment, which limits a president to two elected terms
questions.explanation: Franklin D. Roosevelt's four elections broke the two-term tradition George Washington set. The Twenty-second Amendment, ratified in 1951, wrote the limit into law - no person may be elected president more than twice.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Washington set it, the 22nd locked it.

img.scene: An hourglass on a desk in a formal office beside a window overlooking a capital city. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Washington set it, the 22nd locked it.
img.title: TWO-TERM LIMIT

questions.question: The lawmaking branch of the federal government, created by Article I of the Constitution, is:
questions.correctAnswer: Congress - the Senate and the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: Article I vests 'all legislative powers' in a Congress of two houses - a structure borrowed partly from the Great Compromise of 1787, which balanced population-based and equal state representation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article I, branch one: Congress makes the laws.

img.scene: A grand legislative chamber with two curved banks of empty desks facing a raised rostrum, flags behind it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Article I, branch one: Congress makes the laws.
img.title: ARTICLE I - CONGRESS

questions.question: A representative in the U.S. House serves a term of:
questions.correctAnswer: Two years
questions.explanation: House members face the voters every two years - the shortest federal term - so the chamber closest to the people stays closely answerable to them. Senators serve six years and presidents four, by design.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House: two years, always close to the voters.

img.scene: A calendar-like row of two bright lanterns lit on a porch, the rest dark, dusk in a small town. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House: two years, always close to the voters.
img.title: THE TWO-YEAR HOUSE TERM

questions.question: Every state sends two senators to Washington, but the larger chamber across the Capitol is sized by population and capped by a 1929 law. Counting only its voting seats, that chamber - the House - holds:
questions.correctAnswer: 435 members
questions.explanation: The House has 435 voting members, apportioned among the states by population after each census and fixed at that size by a 1929 law. The Senate's 100 plus the House's 435 make 535 members of Congress in all.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 435 in the House - counted by population.

img.scene: A vast semicircular chamber filled with long curved rows of empty desks stretching far back, symbolic and uncountable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: 435 in the House - counted by population.
img.title: 435 HOUSE MEMBERS

questions.question: To be elected to the U.S. Senate, a candidate must be at least:
questions.correctAnswer: 30 years old, a citizen for nine years, and a resident of the state
distractors: 25 years old and a natural-born citizen
21 years old, like a voter in 1780
questions.explanation: The Senate's qualifications (30 years, nine years a citizen, state residency) are a step above the House's (25 years, seven years a citizen) - the framers meant the smaller chamber to be the more seasoned one.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senate at thirty, House at twenty-five.

img.scene: A marble staircase with broad steps leading up to columned doors, morning sun. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Senate at thirty, House at twenty-five.
img.title: WHO CAN BE A SENATOR

questions.question: In the Senate, the officer who presides and casts the deciding vote when the Senate ties 50-50 is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Vice President of the United States
questions.explanation: The Constitution names the Vice President as President of the Senate, with a vote only when the Senate is equally divided. Day to day, the president pro tempore or junior senators usually hold the gavel, but tie-breaking belongs to the Vice President.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The VP votes only to break the tie.

img.scene: A balanced scale perfectly level on a table in a formal chamber, one chair behind it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The VP votes only to break the tie.
img.title: BREAKING THE TIE

questions.question: Fed up with a corrupt federal judge, a representative introduces articles charging him with bribery and asks the full House to vote on them. Bringing formal charges against a federal official this way is the House exercising its power of:
questions.correctAnswer: Impeachment
questions.explanation: Impeachment is the House's accusation power: a majority vote adopts articles of impeachment, and then the Senate holds the trial. Removing a president takes both steps - the House charges, two-thirds of the Senate convicts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House charges, Senate tries.

img.scene: A procession of officials carrying a sealed document case up marble steps toward a columned building. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: House charges, Senate tries.
img.title: THE POWER TO IMPEACH

questions.question: A bill reaches the President's desk nine days before Congress adjourns for the year. The President sets it aside, signs nothing, and lets adjournment pass with the bill still unsigned. The bill dies by:
questions.correctAnswer: Pocket veto
questions.explanation: A regular veto can be overridden by two-thirds of both houses, but a pocket veto cannot - there is no bill 'returned' to reconsider. It is the one presidential kill Congress has no answer to, and it works only when adjournment prevents return.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Unsigned and adjourned - the bill dies quietly.

img.scene: An envelope resting unopened on an empty desk in a darkened, vacated chamber. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Unsigned and adjourned - the bill dies quietly.
img.title: THE POCKET VETO

questions.question: Congress wants to fund a new bridge but the Constitution requires that bills raising revenue - taxes - must start in the:
questions.correctAnswer: House of Representatives
questions.explanation: The Origination Clause (Article I, Section 7) starts all revenue bills in the House - the chamber closest to the people who pay. The Senate may amend them, and in practice tax bills are negotiated by both, but the first step is the House's.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tax bills begin where voters are closest.

img.scene: A heavy iron key turning in the lock of a treasury vault door, warm lamplight. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Tax bills begin where voters are closest.
img.title: WHERE TAX BILLS BEGIN

questions.question: A senator speaks for many hours to delay a vote on a bill, using the Senate's tradition of extended debate. In the Senate this tactic is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Filibuster - ended on most matters only by a 60-vote cloture motion
questions.explanation: Unlike the House, the Senate historically allowed unlimited debate, so a determined minority could talk a bill to death. Cloture - now 60 votes for most business - is the only way to force an end, which is why 60 became the Senate's practical passing number.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In the Senate, sixty is the working majority.

img.scene: A lone speaker at a podium in a large chamber at night, windows dark, one lamp glowing. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: In the Senate, sixty is the working majority.
img.title: THE FILIBUSTER

questions.question: After each census, states redraw their congressional district maps. Drawing those lines to give one party an unfair advantage is called:
questions.correctAnswer: Gerrymandering
questions.explanation: Redistricting itself is required - districts must hold roughly equal populations. Gerrymandering is the abuse of the process: packing or cracking voters so the map, not the electorate, chooses the winners. The word dates to an 1812 Massachusetts map shaped like a salamander.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Maps should count voters, not choose them.

img.scene: A patchwork of oddly shaped colored fields seen from above, divided by winding streams and roads, no labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Maps should count voters, not choose them.
img.title: GERRYMANDERING

questions.question: The executive branch, headed by the President, has as its chief job to:
questions.correctAnswer: Carry out and enforce the laws Congress makes
distractors: Interpret the laws in court cases
questions.explanation: Article II vests the executive power in the President: enforcing laws, commanding the armed forces, conducting foreign policy and running the departments that administer federal programs day to day.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress writes it; the President runs it.

img.scene: A formal desk with a telephone, a stack of bound volumes and a flag in a bright office. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Congress writes it; the President runs it.
img.title: ENFORCING THE LAWS

questions.question: The President sits down with the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury and the Secretary of Defense for their regular joint briefing. Together with the heads of the other executive departments, this advisory group is known as the:
questions.correctAnswer: Cabinet
questions.explanation: The Cabinet grew from George Washington's four advisers to fifteen department heads today. Members are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and they serve at the President's pleasure.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteen departments advise the President.

img.scene: A long polished table with high-backed chairs in a formal meeting room, flags at the far end. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Fifteen departments advise the President.
img.title: THE CABINET

questions.question: A crisis leaves the presidency and vice presidency vacant on the same day. Under the succession statute Congress passed in 1947, the gavel of the executive passes first to this elected official:
questions.correctAnswer: Speaker of the House
distractors: President pro tempore of the Senate
questions.explanation: The Presidential Succession Act of 1947 puts the Speaker of the House second in line, then the Senate's president pro tempore, then the Cabinet beginning with the Secretary of State. The order was designed to favor elected officials over appointed ones.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Speaker stands second in line.

img.scene: A row of empty high-backed chairs arranged in order along a paneled wall, the first two draped. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Speaker stands second in line.
img.title: LINE OF SUCCESSION

questions.question: A president directs a federal agency to change how a law is enforced, without asking Congress. This written directive is an:
questions.correctAnswer: Executive order
questions.explanation: Executive orders carry the force of law inside the executive branch, but they sit on thinner ice than statutes: Congress can override them by law, courts can strike them down, and the next president can revoke them with a signature.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Orders direct agencies - Congress can answer.

img.scene: A fountain pen resting on a signed document folder on a desk, seal blurred and unreadable, lamplight. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Orders direct agencies - Congress can answer.
img.title: EXECUTIVE ORDERS

questions.question: Before a treaty the President negotiates can take effect, the Constitution requires approval by:
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of the Senate
questions.explanation: The treaty power is shared: the President negotiates and signs, but Article II requires the advice and consent of two-thirds of the senators present. That supermajority is why many modern international deals are made as executive agreements instead.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.

img.scene: Two delegations shaking hands across a long table by tall windows overlooking a river. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate.
img.title: THE TREATY POWER

questions.question: A federal judge issues a ruling so unpopular that crowds demand her removal and newspapers predict she will soon be voted out of office. Why does neither threat work under Article III? Because federal judges hold their offices:
questions.correctAnswer: During good behavior - in practice, for life
questions.explanation: Life tenure (Article III) is the judiciary's shield: a judge who cannot be fired or have pay cut over an unpopular ruling is freer to rule against the government of the day. Judges leave by retirement, death, or impeachment and removal.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life tenure shields unpopular rulings.

img.scene: An empty judge's bench in a quiet wood-paneled courtroom, a single shaft of daylight. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Life tenure shields unpopular rulings.
img.title: LIFE TENURE FOR JUDGES

questions.question: The Supreme Court's power to declare a law unconstitutional - judicial review - was first claimed in the 1803 case:
questions.correctAnswer: Marbury v. Madison
questions.explanation: Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion in Marbury v. Madison reasoned that a constitution judges must swear to uphold cannot coexist with a statute that violates it - so courts must refuse to apply such statutes. Judicial review is inferred from the Constitution, not spelled out in it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury made courts the Constitution's referees.

img.scene: A marble courthouse facade with tall columns and broad steps at midday. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Marbury made courts the Constitution's referees.
img.title: MARBURY V. MADISON

questions.question: A man who cannot afford a lawyer is charged with a felony. Under Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), the state must:
questions.correctAnswer: Provide him a defense attorney at public expense
distractors: Let him borrow money from the court
Try him without a jury instead
questions.explanation: Clarence Gideon's handwritten appeal won a unanimous ruling: the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental, and states must supply a lawyer to defendants who cannot afford one in felony cases. The right later extended to cases carrying possible jail time.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No money for a lawyer? The state provides one.

img.scene: A single sheet of paper and a pencil on a plain table in a small room, a window with bars of soft light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No money for a lawyer? The state provides one.
img.title: GIDEON'S RIGHT TO COUNSEL

questions.question: Police question a suspect in custody without telling him he may stay silent and have a lawyer. His confession is thrown out under the warnings required by:
questions.correctAnswer: Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
questions.explanation: Miranda v. Arizona held that custodial interrogation is inherently coercive, so prosecutors cannot use statements taken without the now-famous warnings: the right to remain silent, and to an attorney, appointed if needed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Silent and counseled - Miranda's two shields.

img.scene: A quiet interrogation room with a table, two chairs and a bright window, no people close to camera. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Silent and counseled - Miranda's two shields.
img.title: MIRANDA WARNINGS

questions.question: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), a unanimous Supreme Court held that in public education, separate facilities for Black and white students are:
questions.correctAnswer: Inherently unequal, violating the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection guarantee
distractors: Acceptable if the buildings are similar
A matter for each state to decide freely
Required by the Constitution's original meaning
questions.explanation: Brown overturned Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine in schooling, ruling that separating children by race generates a feeling of inferiority that unequalizes education itself. The decision lit the legal fuse of the modern civil-rights era.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Separate schools are unequal schools.

img.scene: Children of different backgrounds walking together up the steps of a brick schoolhouse, morning sun. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Separate schools are unequal schools.
img.title: BROWN V. BOARD

questions.question: The first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified together in 1791, are known as the:
questions.correctAnswer: Bill of Rights
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights was the price of ratification: Anti-Federalists feared a strong national government, and the new Congress answered with amendments protecting speech, religion, due process and more against federal power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten amendments answered the ratification debate.

img.scene: Ten tall blank parchment panels hanging in a row in a museum hall, soft spotlights, no writing visible. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Ten amendments answered the ratification debate.
img.title: THE BILL OF RIGHTS

questions.question: Officials in a small town, stung by a newspaper investigation of town spending, try to shut the paper down. A court blocks them, pointing to the amendment that protects a free press - the:
questions.correctAnswer: First Amendment
questions.explanation: The First Amendment bars Congress from abridging freedom of the press - and through the Fourteenth Amendment it binds state governments too. Criticizing officials sits at the very core of what press freedom protects.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Criticizing officials is protected speech.

img.scene: A vintage printing press in a workshop with stacks of blank paper, warm light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Criticizing officials is protected speech.
img.title: FREEDOM OF THE PRESS

questions.question: A town orders a religious group not to meet in the public park while allowing all other groups. This order collides with the First Amendment's:
questions.correctAnswer: Free exercise of religion and freedom of assembly protections
questions.explanation: Singling out a faith for worse treatment attacks free exercise, and banning its gathering attacks assembly - two of the First Amendment's five freedoms, alongside speech, press and petition. The establishment clause limits government sponsorship of religion; the burden here falls on the worshippers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms live in the First Amendment.

img.scene: People of many faiths walking through a public park with trees and a bandstand in autumn light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms live in the First Amendment.
img.title: FREE EXERCISE AND ASSEMBLY

questions.question: Detectives believe stolen goods are hidden inside a suspect's house and want to go in and look. Before they may lawfully enter to search, the Fourth Amendment generally demands a warrant grounded in:
questions.correctAnswer: Probable cause, describing the place to be searched and the things to be seized
distractors: A hunch from an experienced officer
A two-thirds vote of the city council
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment bans unreasonable searches and requires warrants to be specific - no general rummaging. Courts recognize exceptions (a search incident to arrest, plain view, true emergencies), but the warrant-with-probable-cause rule is the default.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no rummage - the Fourth's rule.

img.scene: A front door of a farmhouse with a brass knocker, a garden path, peaceful morning. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no rummage - the Fourth's rule.
img.title: THE FOURTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: 'No person shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself' - this protection against self-incrimination is found in the:
questions.correctAnswer: Fifth Amendment
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment is a bundle: grand jury indictment, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, due process, and just compensation when government takes private property. 'Taking the Fifth' invokes its silence guarantee.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent.

img.scene: A witness stand in an empty courtroom with a microphone and a glass of water, quiet light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent.
img.title: THE RIGHT TO SILENCE

questions.question: A court sets bail at ten million dollars for a minor shoplifting charge. The strongest constitutional objection is the Eighth Amendment's ban on:
questions.correctAnswer: Excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments
questions.explanation: Bail's purpose is to guarantee a defendant's return to court, not to punish before trial. Bail wildly beyond what secures appearance is 'excessive' under the Eighth Amendment, which also bans cruel and unusual punishments after conviction.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bail ensures return - it is not punishment.

img.scene: A set of balance scales tipped absurdly by one enormous weight against a tiny coin, symbolic still life. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Bail ensures return - it is not punishment.
img.title: EXCESSIVE BAIL

questions.question: The Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, passed after the Civil War, are together called the:
questions.correctAnswer: Reconstruction Amendments
questions.explanation: Together they remade American citizenship: the Thirteenth abolished slavery (1865), the Fourteenth defined citizenship and guaranteed equal protection and due process (1868), and the Fifteenth barred denying the vote because of race (1870).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 13 freed, 14 defined, 15 voted.

img.scene: A stone bridge rebuilt after a storm, three new arches standing strong over a river. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: 13 freed, 14 defined, 15 voted.
img.title: RECONSTRUCTION AMENDMENTS

questions.question: A woman registering to vote in 1920 relies on the amendment that barred denying the vote on account of sex - the:
questions.correctAnswer: Nineteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1920 after a seventy-year campaign from Seneca Falls onward, the Nineteenth Amendment doubled the potential electorate at a stroke. Tennessee was the decisive 36th state to ratify.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1920: the vote no longer stops at sex.

img.scene: Women in long dresses and hats marching peacefully down a main street carrying blank banners, period photograph style. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: 1920: the vote no longer stops at sex.
img.title: THE NINETEENTH AMENDMENT

questions.question: A state charges citizens a fee they must pay before voting in a federal election. The Twenty-fourth Amendment makes this practice:
